subject: Degrees of freedom with WLSMV as estimator and experimental data

messages.author: dbbaf8b8ddc8b946
messages.subject: Degrees of freedom with WLSMV as estimator and experimental data
parts:
Hello together,

first thanks to you developers for all the work with the package, it is a great tool! Nevertheless I have some issues and wanted to ask for advice:


I am using the lavaan for conducting path analysis on experimental data. I have two endogenous variables; Y1 represents an behavioral response from the experiment and Y2 represents response on a scale. Y1 can be treated continuous while Y2 should be seen ordinal. Furthermore I have 4 exogenous variables (X1, X2, X3, X4), corresponding to the conditions in the experiment, with 2 levels each. I investigated how the 4 exogenous variables affected the response Y1 and if Y2 has a mediating effect. Based on my assumptions I built the following model:

path.exp <- '
Y1 ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + Y2
Y2 ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4
'

The 4 exogenous variables are coded as dummies with levels 0 and 1. Y2 has values from 1 to 7 and is set to ordered when running the model.

model.full <- sem(path.exp, data, ordered = "Y2", warn = TRUE)

So far so good. Regressions and variances all make sense, but I do not get values for the model fit. This is of course most likely the case because the model is just identified, but I cannot quite understand how the degrees of freedom are calculated. Because when counting on my own (k(k+1)/2) I come to a different result. I already assume that the 6 thresholds for Y2 have to be taken into account, but I am not sure how.


That is why I want to ask how the degrees of freedom are calculated when using ordinal endogenous variables and WLSMV as an estimator.

While I am already posting, I also want to ask whether my apporach seems correct or if I have to account for anything else. As I am dealing with experimental conditions I assume they are not correlated, but lavaan should account for that by default with fixed.x = TRUE.

Any help or suggestions are very welcome.


Thank you very much in advance,
Max

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Degrees of freedom with WLSMV as estimator and experimental data
parts: I investigated how the 4 exogenous variables affected the response Y1 and if Y2 has a mediating effect.
If Y1 and Y2 were both outcomes of the experiment, is it possible for Y2 to have affected Y1?
Y2 has values from 1 to 7 and is set to ordered when running the model.
With this many ordered categories, it is probably better to treat Y2 as continuous.  If it is not approximately normal, you can use a robust estimator.
when counting on my own (k(k+1)/2) I come to a different result. I already assume that the 6 thresholds for Y2 have to be taken into account, but I am not sure how.

There are 6 thresholds observed and estimated, so no df are gained from that part of the model.  The variance of the latent response underlying an ordinal variable is neither observed nor estimated, but its polyserial correlation with other variables is observed and estimated.  Again, no df gained because as you said, your model is saturated.  You can see the number of estimated parameters in the output of 

fitMeasures(model.full, "npar")
how the degrees of freedom are calculated when using ordinal endogenous variables and WLSMV as an estimator.
Still the number of observed summary statistics minus the number of estimated parameters.
As I am dealing with experimental conditions I assume they are not correlated, but lavaan should account for that by default with fixed.x = TRUE.

fixed.x = TRUE means whatever their observed correlation is (including if it is zero, as expected in a balanced design), those values are assumed fixed rather than estimated.  So they are not included in the number of observed summary statistics or estimated parameters.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Degrees of freedom with WLSMV as estimator and experimental data
parts: Thank you very much for the quick and detailed answer!
If Y1 and Y2 were both outcomes of the experiment, is it possible for Y2 to have affected Y1?
Good remark, but in the experimental design as it is, the effect should be unidirectional. So Y2 should not have impacted Y1.
If it is not approximately normal, you can use a robust estimator.

I also first assumed Y2 as continuous, that is why is chose a 7-point scale in the first place. But when running the model with simulated data and with Y2 as ordered I am able to get a better result in terms of regressions parameters and model fit indices. Better result meaning the parameters I input in the simulation and the results I would expect. I am not sure whether it is because treating Y2 with different levels accounts better for the data. Also because I have a large sample size of around 11,000 data points indices get very small.
